newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban backs away from fight with Afghan warlord.
newsitem.headline: Taleban backs away from fight with Afghan warlord.

text.p: Afghanistan's victorious Taleban militia appeared to back away from a standoff with a powerful northern warlord on Wednesday but vowed to attack a former government military chief in his redoubt.
The fundamentalist clerics who took Kabul with hardly a shot fired five days ago were also making overtures towards a sceptical world.

Unexpected support for the Taleban came from the business world. The U.S. energy company Unocal Corp, seeking to build a gas and an oil pipeline across Afghanistan from Turkmenistan to Pakistan, said the victories were a positive development.

Apparently manoeuvring to head off a potential alliance between the only foes they have left, Taleban Acting Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammed Stanakzai told reporters he had no quarrel with northern warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
Stanakzai said an ultimatum delivered by a Taleban field commander to Dostum on Monday was unauthorised.
"Whoever handed over that letter was an enemy to us and Dostum," Stanakzai said.
On Tuesday, former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood's Tajik forces and Dostum's mainly Uzbek soldiers appeared to be exploring an alliance.

Stanakzai spoke as Taleban fighters were squaring off against Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli militia at the mouth of the Salang tunnel, which forms part of the strategic Salang highway, a vital link between Kabul and the north of the country and the former Soviet republics of Central Asia beyond.
Dostum, who controls large portions of northern Afghanistan, had previously managed to distance his forces from the fighting between Taleban and the former Kabul government, which he also opposed.
Tanks, heavy artillery and multiple launch Grad missiles of Dostum were dug in at both ends of the Salang tunnel on Wednesday.
Jumbish-i-Milli frontline commander Colonel-General Chary said there had been no fighting with the Taleban.
He added: "We don't want to fight but we will defend our territory."

The official Kabul Radio monitored in Islamabad on Wednesday said that there had been no clashes so far. But it said Taleban forces had entered the Panjsher valley after turning east from Jabal os-Siraj and capturing the town of Golbahar, 10 km (six miles) away.
It said the Taleban had made some gains during its advance late on Tuesday, but gave no more details.
Panjsher valley is Masood's homeland and scene of his guerrilla exploits against Soviet occupation forces in the 1980s.
A U.N. convoy rolled into Kabul on Wednesday bringing food, medicine, fuel and shelter materials to the most needy residents of the Afghan capital.

Ismail Omar of the U.N. World Food Programme told Reuters 19 trucks from the Pakistani city of Peshawar brought 150 tonnes of wheat flour to feed the infirm, disabled and orphans among the Afghan capital's population of about one million.
He said the WFP was delivering about one-fifth of the city's daily consumption, feeding about 180,000 people.
The United States, which earlier condemned the Taleban for the execution of former president Najibullah, said it would send a diplomat to Kabul for talks with the new rulers.
The envoy will also assess the prospects of re-staffing the U.S. embassy in the Afghan capital, which was evacuated seven years ago, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
He told reporters on Tuesday the diplomat would travel to Kabul in the next couple of days but declined to name the official or say when he would be travelling.

The United States has never broken off diplomatic relations with Afghanistan but pulled out all embassy staff after Soviet forces withdrew from the country in 1989, leading to a civil war between rebel factins that has continued ever since.
Pakistan, which has denied that it supports the Taleban, sent a diplomat to Kabul this week to reopen its embassy.

Russia, which appears to be worried about its border guards who help patrol the uneasy frontier between Tajikistan and Afghanistan, has proposed that leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) meet to work out steps to prevent the upsurge of fighting from spilling into former Soviet territory.

Meanwhile, the United Nations came under attack on Tuesday from the European humanitarin aid Commissioner Emma Bonino for failing to censor Afghanistan over the fate of that country's women under the new Islamic regime established by the Taleban.
The Taleban said last week that it would impose strict fundamentalist limits on women -- making them stop working, stay at home and wear veils in public.

But there were some who welcomed the Taleban's dominance. Chris Taggart, vice president of Unocal International Energy Ventures Ltd, said that "we regard it (the current situation in Afghanistan) as very positive".
"I understand Pakistan has already recognised the (Taleban) government. If the U.S.A follows, it will lead the way to international lending agencies coming in."
